name: Aisha Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Aisha. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and nothing you say will be linked to your name. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a loader underground at Corran, a zinc and lead mine. The loader is what we call an LHD, load-haul-dump: it scoops the broken rock after a blast and carries it to the ore pass, which is a shaft the rock drops down. I'm shift lead for the loader crew on days, so I do the plan at 6, then I'm in the seat most of the shift because we're always short. I'm good at it because I can feel the bucket, I know when it's full without looking at the gauge. What wears me out is the noise, even with plugs and muffs, and the paperwork when someone scrapes a wall.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Tomás, my partner, is a fitter at Corran too, he fixes the loaders I break, which is a running joke. We bought a block of land on the edge of Corran last year, so all our spare money goes on that, and we've got maybe three weeks of savings. Corran pays below the other mines in the region, but it's the only one within an hour. So every dollar we earn comes out of the same hole.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." What goes through your head?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine by me. I use the AI now and then for emails and recipes. If that's all it ever is, okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's useful for small stuff and not much else, which is about what I expected. I'm not someone who gets excited about this or scared of it. I'd probably say that at the dinner table and leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's a relief because of Tomás and me both being at Corran. If something hit the mine, it'd hit us twice. In this picture, nothing hits, so we keep building toward the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am, keep paying off the land, and try to get savings up to a couple of months. Maybe ask about the senior allowance, since I'm doing a lead's job on an operator's rate half the time. Otherwise, same as now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's a boring picture, and boring is good when you're paying off land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you actually use the AI for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly writing incident reports so they sound less angry than I feel. And meal plans for night week, because otherwise I live on toast. It's like a calculator, I use it when it's handy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a lead's job on an operator's rate. How does that come about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The official lead retired in March and they haven't backfilled the role. I've been doing it since, and they keep saying the review is coming. In this picture I'd keep at them politely until it does.

S0.say: It's useful for small stuff and not much else, about what I expected. I don't get excited or scared about it, and I'd say that and leave it there.
S0.think: It's a relief, because Tomás and I both work at Corran and a hit to the mine would hit us twice. In this picture nothing hits, so we keep building toward the house.
S0.do: Keeps working and paying off the land, aiming to build savings to about two months. Politely keeps asking for the lead's allowance she's been owed since March.
S0.feel: Calm; a boring picture is good when paying off land.
S0.quote: It's a boring picture, and boring is good when you're paying off land.
S0.fieldNote: Aisha's main exposure is that both incomes come from one mine, and she raises it straight away. She uses AI casually and without strong feelings. She's quietly owed a lead's allowance, and she pursues it politely rather than angrily.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust." What goes through your head?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Loaders are already going remote. There's a mine two hours south where they run them from a room on the surface.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let's see the numbers before anyone panics. Some of these systems work, some are a mess, and the company will learn which is which. I'd say the union and the company should work out a fair way to move people across.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be worried, because the loader is the obvious one to go remote. And Tomás's job changes too, fixing robots is different from fixing loaders. Both of us at once is the bit that keeps me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once I saw the remote loaders working properly at the other mine, I'd put my name down for the training. I'd push Tomás to do the electrical module so he can fix the new ones. We'd cut back, no new car, no holiday, and put more toward savings instead of the land for a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not falling apart, but it'd be the first thing I think about on the drive in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd wait to see it working. How would you know it's working?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the operators at the other mine still have jobs after a year, and the loaders aren't sitting broken in the workshop. My cousin's husband works there, so I'd just ask him over a barbecue. That's better than any brochure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd pause paying the land. What would that mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means the house is a year later. That's annoying, but it's not the end of anything. I'd rather have a delay than a loan I can't pay when I'm between jobs.

S1.say: Let's see the numbers before anyone panics, because some systems work and some are a mess. The union and company should agree a fair way to move people across.
S1.think: The loader is the obvious one to go remote, and Tomás's fitting job changes too. Both of us at once is what keeps me up.
S1.do: Signs up for remote loader training once she's seen it working at a nearby mine, and urges her partner to take the electrical module. Pauses extra payments on their land for a year to build savings and skips a new car and a holiday.
S1.feel: Anxious; it'd be her first thought on the drive to work.
S1.quote: My cousin's husband works there, so I'd just ask him over a barbecue. That's better than any brochure.
S1.fieldNote: Her public calm contrasts with real private worry about two incomes in one mine. She checks new technology through people she trusts, not company promises. The steady approach is clear: wait for proof, then move quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." What goes through your head?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Both of us out at once, probably. I need a minute with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government and the companies need a plan for mining towns, and they need it now, not in a report in three years. I'm not a protest person, but I'd write to our member of parliament. I'd say it's not about blame, it's about not letting a town fall over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think we're in real trouble. Two incomes from one hole, three weeks of savings, and a block of land we can't build on. I'd be doing sums every night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd sell the land, even at a loss, because it's the only asset we've got. Tomás and I would both take every shift going while the mine still needs us, and bank all of it. Then we'd look at moving to the city near my sister, where at least there are more kinds of work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It'd feel like the floor going soft under the loader, that moment where you know it's going to tip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the short warning time change for you, compared with five or ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years there's no point learning the remote loader, because by 2028 the AI runs it without me. So it's all about money and moving. The longer ones, I'd train. This one, I'd sell up and run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Selling the land, how would that feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Awful. We went out there on a Sunday with a picnic and Tomás paced out where the kitchen would go. Selling that would feel like giving up on us, even though it's just dirt. But dirt doesn't pay rent.

S2.say: The government and companies need a plan for mining towns now, not in a report in three years. It's not about blame, it's about not letting a town fall over.
S2.think: We'd be in real trouble: two incomes from one mine, three weeks of savings, and land we can't build on. I'd be doing sums every night.
S2.do: Sells their block of land in the first month even at a loss, and has both of them work every shift going to bank money. Then plans a move to the city near her sister for wider job options.
S2.feel: Alarmed, like feeling the ground go soft under a loader that's about to tip.
S2.quote: Selling that would feel like giving up on us, even though it's just dirt. But dirt doesn't pay rent.
S2.fieldNote: The two-year picture makes her drop retraining entirely in favour of cash and moving. Selling the land is where her feelings show, through a vivid memory of planning a kitchen. She frames politics as practical planning, not blame.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." What goes through your head?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's tight, but it's workable, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to do this properly, so do it properly. Retraining paid for by the companies, and local, not three hours away. I'd say that at work and to anyone who asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think we have maybe three years of decent work left at Corran, and I'd want both of us out with a new ticket by then. I don't know what work is safe in this picture, but I'd want something you can do in any town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd start a part-time certificate in health and safety, because every site still needs someone signing off, for a while at least. Tomás would do the automation electrical course. We'd keep the land but stop paying extra, and push savings to two months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, still. But it's a manageable anxious, like a hard shift you know will end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the extra three years, compared with two, change for you two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They let us keep the land and still get out. With two years we sell and run. With five we can train, save, and maybe still build a small house, just later. And we'd have a wedding, we keep putting it off, we'd do it small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why health and safety, if AI can do most work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because someone legally has to be responsible when something goes wrong underground. I don't think they'd hand that to a computer straight away. Maybe I'm wrong, but it's the best bet I can see.

S3.say: There's time to do this properly, so do it properly: retraining paid by the companies, and local, not three hours away.
S3.think: We have maybe three years of decent work left at Corran, and I'd want us both out with a new qualification by then, something you can do in any town.
S3.do: Starts a part-time health and safety certificate in year one while her partner does an automation electrical course. Keeps the land but stops extra payments, builds two months of savings, and plans a small wedding.
S3.feel: Anxious but manageable, like a hard shift that will end.
S3.quote: But it's a manageable anxious, like a hard shift you know will end.
S3.fieldNote: With five years, the couple can keep their land and still prepare, which matters a lot to her. Her choice of safety work rests on the idea that someone must be legally responsible. A long-delayed wedding comes into the picture only when there's breathing room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." What goes through your head?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be 37. That feels like a different conversation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's enough time that nobody should be surprised, so let's have a proper plan from the company and the government. Everyone on site should know by year three what's happening to their job. I'd say that at the crew meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think we'd be okay in this one, if we're careful. We could build the house, have the wedding, and still have time to change jobs. The danger is getting comfortable and waiting too long, which is a bit me, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep loading for the first few years, but watch the other mines. Once remote loaders were proven, I'd train on them, and later the safety certificate. We'd build a small house on the land, but a cheaper one than we planned, so the mortgage isn't huge if things change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's a slow worry, not a sharp one. I can live with slow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said waiting too long is a bit you. Can you say more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I like to see things work before I jump, and that's served me well. But with ten years you can tell yourself there's always next year. I'd need Tomás to give me a shove at some point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the smaller house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a big mortgage is a chain. If I have to move for work in 2034, I want to be able to sell or rent it and go. A small house is a choice you can undo.

S4.say: It's enough time that nobody should be surprised, so the company and government need a proper plan. Everyone on site should know by year three what's happening to their job.
S4.think: We'd be okay if we're careful: house, wedding, and still time to change jobs. The danger is getting comfortable and waiting too long, which is a bit me.
S4.do: Keeps loading for a few years while watching other mines, then trains on remote loaders once proven and later on safety work. Builds a smaller, cheaper house than planned so the mortgage stays manageable if they need to move.
S4.feel: Uneasy, a slow worry rather than a sharp one.
S4.quote: Because a big mortgage is a chain.
S4.fieldNote: Aisha knows her own habit of waiting and expects to need a push from her partner. The ten-year picture lets them go ahead with the house and wedding, but she shrinks the house to keep options open. Her plans stay concrete and cautious.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it takes both our jobs at the same time. What would help is a payout that's based on years worked and paid early, and help with rent in whatever town we move to. Something that buys us six months to think.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask couples who work at the same mine. There's a lot of us, because that's how you meet people out here. Nobody plans for both of you losing your job on the same Tuesday.

headlineQuote: Nobody plans for both of you losing your job on the same Tuesday.
portrait: Aisha Costa is a 27-year-old underground loader operator and acting shift lead at a zinc and lead mine, where her partner Tomás is a fitter, so both their incomes come from one mine. They're paying off a block of land on three weeks of savings. She uses AI now and then and waits to see new systems proven before she moves. She's calm in the plateau, anxious in steady disruption, and alarmed by two-year AGI, which would make her sell the land and move. With five and ten years she plans training, a small wedding and a smaller house, while admitting she tends to wait too long.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it would take both her job and her partner's at the same time.
whatWouldHelp: An early payout based on years worked, and rent help in whatever town they move to, enough to buy six months to think.
